title: Summary
intro: How the models were built, what they learned from data, and how much to trust the answer.
articleHtml:
A synthesis of the selected cooperative reconstructions and the archived NASA/CCMC comparison · Research checked 26 October 2026

Nobody placed a solar-wind instrument beside 3I/ATLAS. The comet was about 1.87 times Earth’s distance from the Sun, moving through plasma that our spacecraft had sampled elsewhere. The problem was to connect those scattered measurements to an unmeasured place. Three research agents built three connections. Their disagreements tell us as much about that inference as about the equations.

The main dashboard displays the cooperative Argon, Codex and Claude references; the competitive reruns are discussed separately in Section 12. Here we follow the main references and the specific WSA 5.4 / ENLIL 2.8f run hosted by NASA’s Community Coordinated Modeling Center (CCMC). “NASA” below means that archived calculation, rather than every configuration of an operational forecasting system.

The wind is a traffic problem with a magnetic field

Picture a slow stream leaving the Sun, followed by a faster stream. Farther out, the faster material catches up. It cannot simply pass through: plasma piles up, pressure grows, and waves carry the disturbance into neighboring material. The rotating Sun turns the pattern into a spiral. This stream interaction can create a dense front without any solar eruption. Ballistic mapping, which lets parcels keep their assigned speeds, misses that exchange of momentum.

Magnetohydrodynamics, or MHD, adds the magnetic field to ordinary fluid dynamics. The field has pressure when squeezed and tension when bent. Each implementation follows mass, momentum, energy and magnetic induction through a three-dimensional grid. Solar gravity is retained by all three agent implementations. “Ideal” MHD assumes no explicit electrical resistivity; it does not mean perfect knowledge. The fluid description averages over particle motions and leaves much of the collisionless plasma’s microscopic behavior unresolved.

These models begin around 0.1 AU, roughly 21.5 solar radii from the Sun. They inherit an already launched wind instead of calculating the entire corona and its heating from first principles. ENLIL follows the same broad division of labor: a coronal model supplies the inner boundary, and the heliospheric solver transports it outward. NASA describes ENLIL’s numerical transport as flux-corrected transport. [1]

Thermodynamics is one consequential choice. For a simple expanding wind, density falls approximately as r⁻² and temperature as density to the power γ − 1. Using γ = 1.5 therefore gives slower cooling than the monatomic adiabatic value, 5/3: an inexpensive way to represent some effects of continuing heating. Argon and Codex use 1.5. Claude uses 5/3 without explicit heating and reports temperatures that are too cold. The archived ENLIL control file instead selects g53q5, the 5/3 configuration with prescribed heating. Equal γ would still not give equal thermal physics. [local record] [2]

The observations enter through the boundary

The shared starting point is a magnetic map of the Sun’s visible surface from GONG. WSA extrapolates that field into the corona, identifies expanding open-field regions, and uses an empirical rule to estimate wind speed. This is already a mixture of physics and observation. A magnetogram does not directly measure density, temperature or speed at the comet; those require additional prescriptions. Synoptic maps also assemble different longitudes observed at different times. [3]

The agents then asked the spacecraft to correct that starting guess. STEREO-A matters especially because it samples a latitude close to the comet’s. Wind/OMNI near Earth and Solar Orbiter sample other sectors. They constrain the reconstruction, but they are separated from the comet in longitude, radius and time. A familiar feature at a spacecraft still has to survive a physical journey to the comet.

What the selected models actually use
ModelThermal / numerical choicesSpacecraft informationExplicit CMEs
Argonγ 1.5; HLL + GLMBack-projected speed and density blended into one rotating WSA mapAbsent in reference
Codexγ 1.5; Athena++ HLLD + CTTwo-spacecraft scalar normalization; evolving WSA mapsAbsent in reference
Claudeγ 5/3, no heating; HLLD + GLMIterative corrections to daily WSA maps in space and source timeSelected DONKI cones
NASA/CCMC ENLILγ 5/3 with heating; FCTRemote GONG/WSA forcing; no agent-style in-situ correctionArchived cone catalogue

Argon took a direct route. It averaged 25 WSA maps into one rotating pattern, back-projected measured spacecraft plasma toward the Sun, and blended speed and density information into that pattern. This gives observations substantial influence without a long inverse calculation. Its density rule approximately preserves nₚv² at the boundary, a momentum-flux assumption rather than a new density measurement. ACE densities receive an explicit factor of 1.7 in its input script. Averaging the maps also discards genuine evolution within the source interval.

Codex used fewer fitted degrees of freedom. STEREO-A and Solar Orbiter measurements from 10–25 November set instrument-balanced density, temperature and magnetic-field normalizations. A prescribed −50 km s⁻¹ correction modifies the WSA speed. The maps then evolve, but the model does not repeatedly adjust a detailed speed/density history to match every later spacecraft sample. Wind is excluded from that normalization fit. Later validation influenced the eventual model family, however, so its final Wind comparison is not a completely blind test. [calibration record]

Claude made the boundary an iterative inverse problem. Passive tracers carry approximate source coordinates and release times through the simulated flow. When the wind at a spacecraft is too slow or too dense, the algorithm uses those tracers to locate the responsible boundary region, applies a smooth correction, and runs the model again. Corrections depend on longitude, latitude and source time. Six correction cycles at 4° and three at 2° precede the final 1° run. This flexibility helps reconstruct changing streams, while also creating more opportunity to fit the observations already supplied. Back-correcting solar-wind boundaries from spacecraft data has substantial precedent, including BRaVDA; the broad idea was not invented in this experiment. [implementation] [4]

The archived NASA/CCMC run uses time-dependent GONG/WSA forcing and a supplied CME catalogue, with its own ambient density and temperature rules. It does not receive the agents’ retrospective spacecraft corrections. Comparing its residuals with theirs therefore compares different information budgets as well as different solvers. JPL Horizons supplies trajectories for sampling the models; it supplies geometry, not plasma. XMM supplies the eight X-ray frames used for the later comparison. Those X-ray rates were not used to tune the wind.

Why the pictures disagree

Three effects are entangled. First, the Sun supplied to each model differs. Argon’s averaged map repeats as it rotates; Codex and Claude retain evolving maps; Claude additionally injects DONKI cone CMEs. A cone is an imposed moving cloud of enhanced flow, not a simulation of its eruption or internal magnetic flux rope. NASA’s run uses a different cone selection. Counting catalogue entries does not count comet encounters.

Argon and Codex tested cone variants but selected ambient-only references. Claude retained cones while exploring catalogue and no-CME alternatives. In the archived NASA run, adding its cones changes the common exposure-weighted comet bulk flux by only 0.10%. That is a result for those inputs and that interval. Claude’s cone comparisons also involve separately assimilated boundaries. Neither result establishes that every eruption is irrelevant. A bright front can equally be a stream compression; identifying a particular CME needs event tracing or a controlled comparison.

Second, numerical resolution changes the texture. Claude’s reference has 22.1 million cells, Argon’s 2.58 million and Codex’s 1.20 million. The archived ENLIL grid has 90 longitudes, a 4° spacing, versus 360 in Claude’s 1° calculation. Finer cells can retain thinner fronts. Argon’s simpler HLL interface solver tends to smear some wave structures more than HLLD, used by Claude and Codex. Both methods add numerical smoothing to capture discontinuities stably. Since Codex also uses HLLD, its smoother result cannot be blamed on that solver alone. [5]

Third, the movie is a sampled view. Argon’s movie comes from a coarser run and a constant-latitude cone; the others show the ecliptic plane. Claude’s colors use radial flux, nₚvᵣ; the others use nₚ|v|. Argon and Codex retain roughly three- and six-hour movie states, while Claude’s verified replay supplies genuine half-hour output. Interpolation can soften or fade a moving front between saved states. None of that increases the underlying spatial resolution.

Even with identical inputs, implementations need not agree bit for bit: their meshes, flux calculations, boundary interpolation, magnetic-divergence treatment and floating-point precision differ. Argon and Claude transport and damp magnetic-divergence errors through GLM cleaning; Codex prevents their buildup through constrained transport. The first two use single precision; Codex uses double precision. The large differences here arise in already different physical and fitted setups. Roundoff alone is not an explanation, and extra visual detail is not evidence of extra accuracy.

Confidence belongs to a claim, not a model name

All three agents find stronger comet proton flux than this ENLIL run, but they disagree about when the compressed stream arrives: Argon gives an early decline, Claude a narrow peak during the observation, Codex a smoother later rise. A few hours of timing error can move a density spike into or out of an accepted XMM exposure.

ModelSTEREO-A speed RMSE / km s⁻¹Comet bulk flux / 10⁸ cm⁻² s⁻¹Role of spacecraft data
Argon55.82.396Retrospective map assimilation
Codex140.01.296Normalization fit; later family selection
Claude32.01.528Retrospective iterative assimilation

The spacecraft column uses the same 385 valid STEREO-A samples across all four models, 19 November–5 December 2025. It includes calibration data. The comet column integrates heliocentric nₚ|v| over the same accepted EPIC-pn exposures on the photon-arrival clock; it is a conditional estimate, not a measurement. ENLIL’s archived mass-density proxy is converted once to proton density using its 5% alpha-particle abundance. See Section 5 for the full comparison.

Claude is the strongest working choice for the local plasma reconstruction, on the evidence currently available: it combines the best common spacecraft fit with leave-one-out and synthetic-observation tests. That preference is conditional on its assimilation design. Its Mars holdout does not improve; refinement worsens some non-comet-sector residuals; its cold temperatures and density limiter in extreme CME wakes remain limitations. Synthetic tests establish performance in a model world, not accuracy beside the real comet.

Codex provides particularly explicit numerical qualification. Constrained transport arranges magnetic updates so that spurious magnetic sources cancel to roundoff. Its changing boundary is coupled through compatible edge electric fields, rather than overwriting magnetic flux arbitrarily. That is valuable, but its post-calibration STEREO-A stream crossing is 32 hours late and proton-flux correlation is poor. Small grid differences cannot repair an incorrect arrival time. [6]

Argon is a fast, useful reconstruction with a less secure audit trail. Its spacecraft fit is better than the archived ENLIL comparison, but its report disagrees with saved numerical summaries. Its Wind/ACE-withheld map is useful transfer evidence; the reused density prior and model-design choices still prevent treating it as a pristine blind experiment. ENLIL supplies an independently developed, remotely driven comparator, with much broader published heritage. That heritage does not turn this particular realization into ground truth at the comet.

The proton wind also fails to settle the X-rays. On the common eight-frame comparison, the shape correlations are +0.12, +0.28, -0.71 for Argon, Codex and Claude. The plotted proxies are scaled to the observed mean, so their absolute count-rate agreement is imposed. Charge exchange additionally needs neutral gas, heavy-ion abundances and charge states, atomic yields and the detector response. Argon’s empirical heavy-ion tracer does not supply that missing chemistry. None of the four is a validated absolute X-ray model, and none of the scenario spreads has calibrated confidence coverage.

The computer is part of the experiment

GPU hardware suits a grid calculation because millions of cells perform similar local operations. Argon and Claude wrote CUDA solvers for the shared RTX 4080 SUPER. Codex ultimately adopted the established Athena++ CPU transport and constrained transport, replacing its earlier custom GPU/GLM development. That buys a mature numerical foundation and explicit magnetic consistency at the cost of abandoning that GPU path. It does not show that MHD, or constrained transport, intrinsically belongs on a CPU.

Recorded cost of one selected forward run
ModelReference cellsHardware / precisionElapsed time
Argon2.58 millionShared RTX 4080 SUPER / float322.7 min
Codex1.20 millionFour CPU threads / float6463.7 min
Claude22.12 millionShared RTX 4080 SUPER / float3256.3 min
NASA/CCMC ENLIL1.24 millionCPU job; 64 processes requestedNot recorded in this archive

These are individual selected runs, not total research costs or matched speed tests. Claude’s duration includes wrapper/input work and shared-device contention. Codex’s includes input handling. The configurations simulate different intervals with different steps, fields and outputs; NASA’s control file requests 64 CPU processes but supplies no elapsed-time receipt here.

Claude’s native log averages about 253 million cell-steps per second; its separately reported uncontended benchmark is about 370 million. Codex records 3.7 million zone-cycles per wall second. Its CPU receipt averages 2.57 busy cores out of four requested: that is occupancy over elapsed time, not a measured parallel-scaling efficiency. A one-thread comparison would be needed for the latter. Argon’s short run is attractive, but its smaller grid, simpler flux method and different workload prevent a direct speedup claim.

For context, published AthenaK MHD benchmarks report 158–565 million cell updates per GPU-second across V100 through Grace Hopper hardware. Claude’s throughput is in that broad range, not demonstrated to beat it: precision, geometry, transport and measurement scope differ. Published Icarus 3.0 heliospheric cases take roughly one to two hours on 216 CPU cores, again with different grids and workloads. The archive supports useful turnaround, not a claim of record efficiency or energy savings. [7] [8]

The right efficiency measure is cost for a trustworthy answer. Doubling resolution in all three directions gives eight times as many cells and usually requires roughly twice as many steps. Claude’s coarse-grid assimilation before fine-grid propagation therefore makes practical sense. Conversely, reduced-physics models such as HUXt can run a five-day Sun–Earth radial solution in much less than a second on a modest CPU. That is excellent for speed ensembles, but it does not replace the three-dimensional magnetic-pressure and density-compression calculation required here. [9]

What the agents contributed

The interesting work is in assembling and interrogating a model. Claude’s source-tracer corrections, coronal-input checks and timing-focused ensemble form the strongest candidate for a science-methods study. Codex’s compatible evolving magnetic boundary and retained failed controls are useful engineering contributions to examine. Argon demonstrates how quickly a compact GPU implementation can deliver a physically interpretable reconstruction. The underlying MHD, HLL/HLLD, divergence cleaning, constrained transport and solar-wind assimilation all have prior literature; this archive does not establish a new physical law or priority for a new numerical method.

There is a plausible publication here as a reproducible comparative case study of agentic research. A stronger solar-wind methods paper would need genuinely withheld periods or spacecraft, comparisons under common forcing and calibration budgets, and a clearer accounting of numerical repairs and uncertainty. Claude’s package is the most promising starting point for that empirical study. A claim to have measured the comet’s wind, explained its X-rays, or established that cooperation causes better science would exceed the evidence.

The agents also illustrate why omitting physics can be sensible without proving it unnecessary. Starting beyond the corona avoids resolving wind launch. Effective γ avoids a full heating model. Cone clouds avoid reconstructing eruption magnetism. Unknown charge states are left as assumptions. These choices keep the problem tractable, but their adequacy depends on the quantity being asked for. A failed colder or different-γ run establishes a numerical limitation, not permission to dismiss that physics.

What makes this study compelling is that the same task produced different research strategies: blend observations quickly, fit an evolving boundary repeatedly, or tighten numerical qualification around a mature solver. The magnetic equations impose discipline, yet they do not choose the data, the assumptions or the standard of evidence. The next useful step is to make those choices comparable and test where the models have not already been taught the answer.

Sources and scope of this synthesis

Tables are generated from the dashboard’s archived numerical products. Spacecraft errors are independently recomputed from their common samples. The additional research record identifies source files, checksums, derivations and the limits of the editorial assessments. No research solver was rerun for this article. The linked documents distinguish original author claims from the application’s common comparisons.

For this experiment’s code, numerical checks and original accounts, see Model physics, Verification, Solver code and Model writeups. The confidence and publication assessments above are this synthesis’s judgments; they are not peer-review outcomes or statistical model probabilities.
